title_en: The Doctrines Distinctive to the Rabbanites, in Which All the Jewish Sects Dissent from Them — Save Those Who Followed Them Among the Outsiders — Including Matters in Which They Dissented from the Text of Scripture and Contradicted Their Own Statements

segments.en: We opened by recalling those [sects] only because we have already said that the very duties in which they dissented are the ones inherited from Jeroboam, and that he is the first to bring dissension into the religion. We have already recounted what Scripture reports of what Jeroboam dissented in, and we made it a proof that the nation — at the time it was exiled — stood upon his doctrines, that it was scattered through the world while upon those doctrines, and that it inherits them down to this day; and these are the doctrines of the Rabbanites and their lax rulings.

Let us begin with what they say of the Creator — exalted be His mention. They have permitted concerning Him likeness and corporealization (al-tashbīh wa-l-tajsīm), described Him with the contraries of [proper] descriptions, [held] that He has limbs and a measure, and fixed the measure of each of His limbs — how long it is and how broad. This is found among them in a book they call Shiʿur Qomah ("the Measure of the Stature") — meaning the stature of the Creator, exalted and magnified — besides what they mention of Him in the Talmud and elsewhere of their books, of tales and acts and other matters unfitting even for some of creation, let alone for the Creator, exalted. We shall mention a great deal of this later.

They further claim that this Torah in the nation's hands is not the Torah that Moses — peace be upon him — brought, but is rather what Ezra composed; for the one that Moses brought, they claim, was lost, fell away, and vanished. This is to bring down the religion utterly. Had the Muslims taken up this statement of the Rabbanites, it would have been a great proof in their hands and an argument for them; for some of their controversialists already argue against us, saying that the Torah you possess is not the Torah Moses brought — and we conclude against whoever among them argued this that he has lied and contradicted himself, and that what drove him to it was vainglory and the laying of an objection against us. But had they grounded it on the Rabbanites' own statement, they would have had a broad answer and would have needed nothing else.

Of this also: that they discarded prayer from the "Book of Psalms" and made it instead from what they themselves composed. This contradicts what Scripture reports, for it says [Ezra 3:10]: "לְהַלֵּל אֶת ה' עַל יְדֵי דָּוִיד מֶלֶךְ יִשְׂרָאֵל." And yet they say at the head of their prayer: "אֲשֶׁר בָּחַר בְּעַבְדּוֹ דָוִד וְרָצָה בְּשִׁירוֹתָיו…," and the rest of the formula. So they have admitted by this saying that praise and laud of God — exalted be His praise — is an obligation from David's words. Yet they did not take it up as it ought to be taken; rather they say it while seated, merely by way of recitation and mention. We shall complete the matter with proof in its place.

They forbade people to press their faces to the ground when prostrating. This contradicts the saying of Scripture [2 Chr 7:3]: "וַיִּכְרְעוּ אַפַּיִם אַרְצָה עַל הָרִצְפָה וַיִּשְׁתַּחֲווּ." Moreover, at the end of the prayer they do what the Christians do, bowing right and left, claiming that this bow is to the two angels appointed over each person, one on a man's right and the other on his left. More astonishing still: they begin with the bow toward [the angels], and only afterward bow to the Creator — magnified and glorified — which is the bow toward the front.

With this, they ask the angels to convey their prayers to the Creator — exalted and exalted — that they may make Him hear their supplications and [pleas for] mercy. This is in their saying: "מַכְנִיסֵי רַחֲמִים, הַכְנִיסוּ רַחֲמֵינוּ לִפְנֵי בַּעַל הָרַחֲמִים." They have interpreted in this sense the saying of Solomon [Eccl 10:20]: "אַל תְּקַלֵּל מֶלֶךְ בְּמַדָּעֲךָ" — claiming he meant by it the Creator, magnified and glorified — and his saying [ibid.]: "וּבַעַל הַכְּנָפַיִם יַגֵּיד דָּבָר" they referred to the mention of the angels, of whom it is said [Isa 6:2]: "שֵׁשׁ כְּנָפַיִם שֵׁשׁ כְּנָפַיִם לְאֶחָד." So they claim that Scripture reports thereby concerning the Creator — far exalted is He above this! He it is who described Himself in saying [Jer 32:27]: "הִנֵּה אֲנִי ה' אֱלֹהֵי כָּל בָּשָׂר, הֲמִמֶּנִּי יִפָּלֵא כָּל דָּבָר?" and says [ibid. 32:17]: "לֹא יִפָּלֵא מִמְּךָ כָּל דָּבָר"; and of whom it is said [Dan 2:22]: "הוּא גָּלֵא עַמִּיקָתָא וּמְסַתְּרָתָא, יָדַע מָה בַחֲשׁוֹכָא." Does One whose description is this stand in need that a statement or speech reach Him or be conveyed to Him?

Of this: they permitted on the Sabbath that a man ask of his fellow a jar of wine and a jar of oil; this is in their saying [M. Shabbat 23:1]: "שׁוֹאֵל אָדָם מֵחֲבֵרוֹ כַּדֵּי יַיִן וְכַדֵּי שֶׁמֶן, וּבִלְבַד שֶׁלֹּא יֹאמַר לוֹ הַלְוֵנִי, וְכֵן הָאִשָּׁה מֵחֲבֶרְתָּהּ כִּכָּרוֹת. וְאִם אֵינוֹ מַאֲמִינוֹ, מַנִּיחַ טַלִּיתוֹ אֶצְלוֹ, וְעוֹשֶׂה עִמּוֹ חֶשְׁבּוֹן לְאַחַר הַשַּׁבָּת." This is buying and selling on the Sabbath in fact — only that it is a stratagem (ḥīla), as he said [Jer 9:4]: "הַעֲוֵה נִלְאוּ." And concerning the "ʿeruv ḥaṣerot" they said what is famous and known to everyone.

They permitted a man to write on the Sabbath one letter or two, provided it is not a complete name or a single [whole] word. As though, had he written "dalet–nun" intending the name "Dan," he would be a sinner, since it is a complete name; but had he written "dalet–nun" intending part of the letters of "Daniel," he would not be a sinner, since he did not write a complete name. Likewise they permitted a weaver to weave into a garment one thread or two from which no folded [piece] results — that is, a portion of a garment.

They permitted intercourse on the day of the Sabbath, in which there are three things contrary to what we were commanded concerning the Sabbath: the first — motion and exertion, contrary to [Exod 20:10]: "לֹא תַעֲשֶׂה כָל מְלָאכָה"; the second — the contracting of impurity, contrary to the sanctity that is obligatory on the Sabbath; the third — the emission of seed, contrary also to His saying [Exod 34:21]: "בֶּחָרִישׁ וּבַקָּצִיר תִּשְׁבֹּת."

They permitted these things whose contrary is manifest, and forbade things whose very opposite the senses attest. Of this: that a man should not prostrate on the day of the Sabbath — lest he ask of his Lord a need, there being no prayer that they or others pray that does not contain the asking of needs. How is it permitted that a man ask his Lord a need standing or seated, and not permitted that he ask while prostrate? And how is it permitted that he say in his prayer: "תּוֹלֶה רַחֲמֶיךָ וְתָאֶת כַּעַסְךָ, וְהַצִּילֵנוּ וְכָל בְּנֵי יִשְׂרָאֵל מִדֶּבֶר וַעֲוֹנוֹת" — which is the asking of needs for himself and for all the House of Israel — yet not permitted that he ask a need for himself alone?

More astonishing than this — that they claim in the "halakha" that what the gentiles have sown and planted becomes pure by their drawing near to it; for they did it in the name of idolatry, and Scripture has said [Isa 30:22]: "וְתִזְרֵם כְּמוֹ דָוָה" — which requires that eating it be forbidden, and that the Children of Israel, on entering the land of al-Shām, ate neither of its crops nor of its fruits. With what heart do they bear this?

They likewise forbade a man to bring his hand to his mouth (to eat) while walking less than four cubits — yet one does not know the ruling on urine and excrement! Is there in [all] doctrines anything more frivolous than this doctrine?

It is a wonder that they forbade a man to put straw in a sieve on the day of the Sabbath — lest a speck of straw fall through the sieve, so that he would be as one who sifted on the Sabbath — yet permitted one whose roof-beam broke on the Sabbath to bring a board and place it under that beam to prop it up. Is there a stronger self-contradiction than this — that they forbade what is unintended, and permitted the [very] intention itself?
They also permitted a man to cook on the Sabbath — by preparing the pot before the Sabbath and setting it in the oven — so that it cooks on the Sabbath and is eaten on the Sabbath.
Of this: they made obligatory the circumcision of a dead [infant], which reason rejects in the utmost.

Of this: they abolished impurity for all people in the Exile. This is in their saying: "מִשֶּׁחָרַב הַבַּיִת, לֹא טוּמְאָה וְלֹא טָהֳרָה." They claimed there is none impure from leprosy nor pure from [contact with] the dead, and by this saying brought down all the [laws of] impurity. For with them — if the corpse, which is the gravest of impurities, yields no purification, then all people in this age are impure, and they are not on guard concerning what they have touched or contacted of the other impurities. For if the grave impurity has befallen them, and they have no cleansing or purification from it, then what is below it already envelops them; yet they pray, touch the scrolls and the "holy [writings]," and this for them is impermissible. In this connection they spoke words that contradict this saying: they claimed that they permitted the impure to touch the scrolls — because the scrolls are written on impure hides, being from the beasts of the gentiles. We say to them: why did you permit scrolls to be written on the hides of gentiles — when in this permission you have joined impurity and purity? They claimed they did so in order that scrolls might be plentiful in people's hands, and that had they permitted scrolls to be written only on Jewish hides, scarcely a scroll or sheet of the Torah would be found, and reading would dwindle in the nation. Do you not see the clear flaw in this? — for we know that in a single city there is already found, of the hides that Jews slaughter, what would suffice for all the scrolls and books of the world! We also said to them: is it not possible that among the scrolls are some whose hides are from a Jew's beasts? Why have you mixed everything into a single rank?

They further contradicted what they made obligatory concerning the abolition of corpse-impurity in this age — that there is no purification from it — from another angle: that they forbid the priests to draw near to the dead or to carry corpses to the graves. For if there is no impurity and no purity, but all people are impure, and they pray and read the books and scrolls nonetheless, the impurity that befell them not preventing them — what is this special status by which the priests must be singled out for this prohibition? If they excuse themselves by the saying of Scripture [Lev 21:2]: "כִּי אִם לִשְׁאֵרוֹ הַקָּרֹב אֵלָיו" — the answer is that this dispensation took effect only when there was something by which purification could be had; so why have you permitted it now, when purification is not to be found?

More astonishing than this — that the corpse of one of the gentiles, with them, does not convey impurity. This contradicts what Scripture reports, that the Children of Israel were commanded to become impure from the people of Midian, in His saying [Num 31:19]: "וְאַתֶּם חֲנוּ מִחוּץ לַמַּחֲנֶה שִׁבְעַת יָמִים." They excused this claim by saying that Scripture said [Num 19:14]: "אָדָם כִּי יָמוּת בְּאֹהֶל"; they said: "adam [man] means only Israel," per His saying [Ezek 34:31]: "וְאַתֵּן צֹאנִי, צֹאן מַרְעִיתִי, אָדָם אַתֶּם." They further claimed that one who touched a corpse's bone — if it is broken — does not become impure, per His saying [Num 19:16]: "אוֹ בְעֶצֶם אָדָם" — woe to whoever said this! Did he not know that the part of a bone is bone, even if it is a fragment of it, just as the finger is a part of flesh and is flesh?

They said [M. Niddah]: "מֻתֶּרֶת הָאִשָּׁה הַנִּדָּה לְשַׁמֵּשׁ בְּכָל צָרְכֵי הַבַּיִת," and said in the Talmud [Ketubbot 4b]: "כָּל מְלָאכוֹת שֶׁהָאִשָּׁה עוֹשָׂה לְבַעְלָהּ, נִדָּה עוֹשָׂה לְבַעְלָהּ" — meaning that all a wife may do for her husband, a menstruant may do: cooking, baking, handling clothes and vessels, and the rest. Yet they specified three things they did not permit her: that she not spread his bed, not light his lamp, and not mix his cup. So they permit her to cook and bake for him what he eats, but do not permit her to light the lamp — in which there is neither harm nor benefit nor impurity clinging to a person. And concerning the "seven days of purity" they said what God did not command.

Graver than this is your saying that only the priest recognizes a [genital] flux (zivah), and that the woman — if she saw the blood — would convey it to him until he should tell her whether it is menstrual blood or flux-blood. They relied on the saying of Scripture [Deut 17:8]: "בֵּין דָּם לְדָם," which no one possessed of sense — let alone of full reason — would doubt was meant only as a distinction between healthy blood and diseased blood. They claimed that the one with a flux is not reckoned a full flux-sufferer until he sees the flux three times — which God did not say.

Of this: that if the impure is mixed with sixty times its measure of the pure, the pure does not become impure from that impurity and is not forbidden. With them — if a dead mouse or pork fell into wine or vinegar of sixty times its measure, and then was crushed and dispersed, eating and drinking the thing it fell into is not forbidden. By this saying they eat the impure outright. Likewise they permitted the worm that breeds in fruit, flesh, fish, and beans, and all the like — this being as the first, or graver. They permitted the fat-tail (alyah) explicitly forbidden among the [forbidden] fats, and likewise the kidneys and the lobe of the liver.

Of this: their permitting of the "ben pequʿa," and their saying that even had it plowed a field for five years, the slaughter of its mother would render it pure. With them — had a ewe or cow been slaughtered when the time of its bearing had come, and its belly then cut open and a young one come forth that lived five years — that young one needs no slaughter for whoever wishes to eat it, and nothing of it is forbidden at all. By this saying they have permitted seven of the forbidden things: first — carrion; second — blood; third — fat; fourth — a limb from the living; fifth — "it and its young"; sixth — the slaughter of a non-Jew; seventh — the sciatic nerve. And it follows for them by this saying that if a ewe or cow died at the time of its bearing before it gave birth, and its belly was then cut open and the young came forth alive and then lived as long as it lived — its eating would never be permitted; for it is part of the dead, and what was part of the dead may not be eaten. For if its mother's slaughter purified it and permitted it, this requires that its mother's death rendered it impure and forbade it.

They permitted all this, and forbade what God did not forbid and for which no root is found — namely what they claimed of the "ṭerefot" discernible by inspecting the lung, and what they mentioned of the conditions of slaughter in the "law of slaughter" (sharīʿat al-shaḥṭ), which are: pausing (shehiyah), pressing (derasah), burrowing (ḥaladah, of the knife), tearing (hagramah, the knife's deviation), and slaughter with a notched knife. In all these they dissented from the saying [Deut 13:1]: "לֹא תֹסֵף עָלָיו וְלֹא תִגְרַע מִמֶּנּוּ."

Among the wonders — what they made obligatory of restricting the [amount of] flesh, which the reports of Scripture refute, for they [show] the multitude of offerings on [festal] occasions, such as His saying [1 Kgs 3:4]: "וְהֶעֱלָה שְׁלֹמֹה אֶלֶף עֹלוֹת," and like the Passover and the rest. Would any sensible person accept that all this had someone to consume it, or that there was at any time what could bear it? Does any doubter doubt that most of these things were done only by way of a symbolic act?

More wondrous still — that they forbade putting the meat in the pot in cold water except after the water has boiled; for they claimed that if meat is put into cold water and then the whole is boiled, the blood dissolves into the water and is consumed; but if the water is boiled and the meat then put in, it does not dissolve into it. From this saying of theirs it follows that eating the blood within the very flesh is permitted, but in the broth forbidden. The like seals upon them in their forbidding the cooking of the liver and the spleen — for they permit eating them roasted. Similar is that they permit roasting the fish whole and cooking it with its blood and eating it; but if the blood came out of it without disturbance, its blood is forbidden to eat. They permitted eating the floating dead fish, explicitly [declared] carrion — to the point that they claimed that if a dead, impure fish was caught and a pure fish found in its belly, eating the pure one is permitted. This they permitted, and forbade meat with milk.

They claimed that the bones of carrion and of a ṭerefah, and their hide, are not forbidden to eat; rather, only eating the flesh is forbidden, per His saying [Exod 22:30]: "וּבָשָׂר בַּשָּׂדֶה טְרֵפָה לֹא תֹאכֵלוּ." It then follows for them that they should permit eating the bones and hide of swine, if Scripture forbade only eating its flesh. Likewise it follows concerning the fat, the liver, the spleen, the lung, and the marrow — that none of these is forbidden, since none of them is flesh, and only eating the flesh was forbidden. And if it were obligatory that all these be forbidden by analogy to the flesh, then eating the hide and bone would be forbidden too, by analogy to the flesh.

They admitted that the heads of the months used to be fixed by sighting the moon, and dissented from this by fixing them through the intercalation of the month (ʿibbur) built on the rule "not on [days] 2, 4, 6," for which no obligating cause is known; it is what "Isaac son of Bakhī" did. Hai, head of the academy, already mentioned this in a book he composed, as did [other] people, concerning the intercalation of the month. The rule "not on 2, 4, 6" has two [explanations]: some claim they did it so that the seventh day of the Festival of Booths should not fall on the Sabbath — for [otherwise] the gifts and offerings would be withdrawn, since it was the practice of those who attended the Temple to give the gifts on the seventh day of the Festival of Booths, and if it fell on the Sabbath, there would be a defect and disruption in this. Others claim they did it so that the Day of Atonement should not fall on a Friday or a Sunday; for if a death occurred on Friday — which was the Day of Atonement — and a Sabbath preceded it, or a death on the Sabbath followed by the Day of Atonement, the corpse would remain two days and two nights and putrefy.

They claimed that [Num 33:3] "מִמָּחֳרַת הַפֶּסַח," on which the Children of Israel went out of Egypt, was the sixteenth of Nisan — contrary to the text's saying [ibid.]: "וַיִּסְעוּ מֵרַעְמְסֵס בַּחֹדֶשׁ הָרִאשׁוֹן," and His saying [ibid.]: "מִמָּחֳרַת הַפֶּסַח יָצְאוּ בְנֵי יִשְׂרָאֵל" on the fifteenth day of the month. Likewise they claimed that what remained of the Passover was burned on the sixteenth of Nisan, contrary to His saying [Exod 12:10]: "וְהַנֹּתָר מִמֶּנּוּ עַד בֹּקֶר בָּאֵשׁ תִּשְׂרֹפוּ."

Of their self-contradictions: they claimed that one who has an uncircumcised person in his house may not eat the Passover. Yet they claim that the Children of Israel used to slaughter the Passover for forty years in the wilderness, and among them was a group of the uncircumcised — namely those born in the wilderness, per His saying [Josh 5:7]: "כִּי עֲרֵלִים הָיוּ, כִּי לֹא מָלוּ אוֹתָם בַּדָּרֶךְ."

They permitted leaven to be brought into a Jew's house during the seven days of unleavened bread, if it is not his own — by there being in his house a man not of the religion's people, for whom, as an "outsider," it is permitted to bring leaven into the Jew's house. They excused themselves by His saying [Exod 13:7]: "לֹא יֵרָאֶה לְךָ חָמֵץ"; they said: this forbids it to you, but to another than you it is not forbidden. In this sense there are two kinds of corruption: the first, that it contradicts the text, for He says [ibid. 12:19]: "לֹא יִמָּצֵא בְּבָתֵּיכֶם"; the second, that in this they contradict themselves, for they forbade our having leaven in another's house alongside Scripture's saying "בְּבָתֵּיכֶם." For if by His saying "לְךָ" He forbids only to you and not to another, then by His saying "בְּבָתֵּיכֶם" He forbids only what is in our houses and not in the houses of others.

They made obligatory the seeking of the new barley (aviv) and the taking of the Passover upon it — and contradicted this by their saying concerning the intercalation of the month. I shall recount some of what is in their books that brings the matter down, and this is in the Seventh Maqala, in which the heads of the months and the new barley are treated.

Among what they dissented in against the text plainly: Scripture made obligatory concerning the "goring ox" that if it killed a person, its owner is put to death, per [Exod 21:29]: "וְהַשּׁוֹר יִסָּקֵל וְגַם בְּעָלָיו יוּמָת" — yet they claimed he is not put to death.

They discarded the standing [daily] prayer (the morning tamid) on the Day of Atonement, for whose obligation there is no support; for they open with the afternoon prayer of the Day of Atonement and follow it with the "additional" (musaf). They made obligatory a prayer that is not known — the one they call the prayer of "neʿilah," which they pray at the end of the day.

They claimed that the time of the aṣīl is from midday to sunset, and then contradicted this by saying in the "Mishnah" [Negaʿim 2:2] that the leper is not inspected at dawn, nor at midday, nor at the two declines [of the sun], but is inspected in the seventh hour, the eighth, and the ninth. This indicates that those three hours are not of the time of the aṣīl that they claimed to be from midday to sunset.

They did not make obligatory — if two or three "additional" [prayers] fall on a single day, such as the New Year falling on a Sabbath, where three "additionals" would be obligatory: the additional of the Sabbath, of the New Moon, and of the New Year — they did not make obligatory of the three more than a single prayer in which the three matters are mentioned. And if this is permitted, it would have been permitted that these be mentioned in the standing [daily] prayer, with no need for another prayer. So they contradicted the obligatory prayers, and made obligatory an added prayer they called the prayer of [the afternoon].

Scripture said [Lev 23:40]: "וּלְקַחְתֶּם לָכֶם בַּיּוֹם הָרִאשׁוֹן" — commanding the taking of [certain] things for making the booth, as was interpreted and explained in Ezra [Neh 8:15]; yet they claimed it is only for the willow branch, and that the "taking" is only a taking in the hand. Scripture made obligatory the keeping of the festival-day one day in each festival — they made it two days. Likewise it made obligatory the eating of unleavened bread seven days, and dwelling in the booth seven days — they made them eight.

Of this, their saying: that one who died childless, his inheritance went to his brother, who would do the levirate to his wife, and to none else. Likewise, that one who died leaving a young daughter together with a son, [the daughter] must take a tenth of the inheritance; but if she was of age, she must take nothing at all of her father's property, and is left to die of hunger. What cause is it that distinguished between the minor and the adult [daughter] in inheritance? Is this ruling not in the category of [Hab 1:4]: "יֵצֵא מִשְׁפָּט מְעֻקָּל"?

As for the people of al-Shām — they made obligatory examination by the finger (before intercourse), and whoever submitted to the argument for it claimed that it is obligatory only so that a man not proceed to engage in something forbidden; for he does not know whether the woman he wishes to lie with is sound and clean, or has already engaged in something forbidden and corrupt. If she did so and he then came to her, he would have come upon something forbidden; but if he examined her with the finger, he would be safe from engaging in the forbidden. We say to the holder of this saying: if this is obligatory, then by its [logic] it follows that a man is obliged — every time he wishes to come to his wife — to test her with the "water of the suspected adulteress" (mei sotah); for he is not secure that she has not already engaged in corruption! So that — if he came to her without testing — he would have come upon the forbidden; and the whole House of Israel would then need to lock up their wives every single day until they bring them to the Temple, and only then engage with them, and to separate from them their nights and days! Rather, what we have said is more fitting and more binding than what they said and made obligatory: namely, that he who wishes to lie [with her] should ascertain the woman's soundness or corruption from the moment he begins with her, before the completion of the act — and then, if he saw the matter to be improper, he could properly abstain from the act.

They said of the unmarried woman — who is the unattached one: if she was alone with [several] men, some of whom are permitted to marry her and some not — that is, her [forbidden] kin — and one of them came to her and she bore a child: if she said the child is from the forbidden kin, the child is a "mamzer"; but if she said it is from those permitted to marry her, the child is legitimate. We say to them: glory be to God! Is it permitted that her statement and testimony be accepted, when she herself is a fornicatress?

They claimed that if a man's wife bore a child: if that child was from a non-Jew or a Jewish slave — whether she was compelled by one of them or [willingly] submitted — the child is legitimate. They made the Jewish slave like a non-Jew, [yet] he is subject to the commandments, and obligatory upon him is [Lev 20:10]: "מוֹת יוּמַת הַנֹּאֵף וְהַנֹּאָפֶת" — his ruling is the ruling of the native-born.
They said that one who raped a woman and lay with her may marry her daughter, contrary to [Lev 18:17]: "עֶרְוַת אִשָּׁה וּבִתָּהּ לֹא תְגַלֵּה."

[The text here is partly corrupt.] They permitted marrying the half-sister from a foreign mother or from another [father]; and an analogy follows for them in this, since the divorced woman, if she fornicated, may not return to her husband, per His saying [Jer 3:1]: "וְאַתְּ זָנִית רֵעִים רַבִּים, וְשׁוֹב אֵלַי, נְאֻם ה'." [They named some fifteen women freed by the death [of a relative] and by the loosing of the sandal — the daughter, the son's daughter, the daughter's daughter, and the rest of the [forbidden] kin — yet permitted others by analogies that contradict the very prohibitions.]

They said concerning [Jer 17:22]: "וְלֹא תוֹצִיאוּ מַשָּׂא מִבָּתֵּיכֶם" — that carrying out and bringing in on the Sabbath is forbidden. Then they said: one who carried from one domain to another is not a sinner unless his hand carried a thing from one place to another place and set it down in another place. But if his hand was outstretched and a man placed a purse in it, and he drew his hand from domain to domain, he is not a sinner. Then they explained this in the "Mishnah" [Shabbat 1:1]: "יְצִיאוֹת הַשַּׁבָּת שְׁתַּיִם שֶׁהֵן אַרְבַּע."

They said concerning [Exod 21:15]: "וּמַכֵּה אָבִיו וְאִמּוֹ" — that he is not a sinner unless he strikes them both together; but if he struck them separately, he is not [liable]. So too with cursing. And they said of [Deut 21:18] "בֵּן סוֹרֵר וּמוֹרֶה" — that there never was and never will be [such a case]. This shows that whoever founded this saying is either trifling or a fool.

They said: one who vowed a vow and regretted it goes to a sage to absolve him of his vow, per their saying [Ḥagigah 10b]: "הוּא אֵינוֹ מַתִּיר אֶת נִדְרוֹ, אֲבָל אֲחֵרִים מַתִּירִין." They said in the "Halakhot Gedolot": one who has a vow or oath upon him and wishes to be released — goes to the Rabbanites that they absolve him, if the one who vowed says, "I did not swear with [such-and-such] intent," and then they absolve him for it. Of them is the saying [Ps 89:35]: "וּבְרִיתִי לֹא אֲחַלֵּל" — and is this permitted to another than Him? Did He not say [Zech 5:4]: "הוֹצֵאתִיהָ, נְאֻם ה' צְבָאוֹת"?

They claimed that one who consummated [a marriage] may not return to intercourse except after seven days — lest menstrual blood come out with the blood of the [broken] hymen, so that he would have come upon a menstruant. We say to them in this: if this is obligatory, then it follows that he becomes impure every time he draws near her during those seven days — for he is not secure that she is not a menstruant.

Of this — their permitting the brother's daughter and the sister's daughter, between whom and the paternal aunt and daughter-in-law there is no difference; for reason does not distinguish between the [paternal] uncle and aunt and the maternal uncle and aunt.

What is more astonishing than that one blesses over the lamp of the Sabbath eve, claiming in his blessing that God commanded it? Likewise the lamp of the festival of Ḥanukkah. More astonishing still — their saying concerning the compounding of the incense. That is: the incense which Scripture reported to be of four things [Exod 30:34], "נָטָף וּשְׁחֵלֶת וְחֶלְבְּנָה, סַמִּים וּלְבֹנָה זַכָּה" — they added [more] things, namely: balsam, musk, sandalwood, and floating-storax. Likewise, Scripture reported that they should be equal parts — yet they made some of them seven, some nine, and some three.

They have, in the laws of marriage, manifestly ugly and corrupt matters whose exposition would be lengthy. I have left off pursuing that, for brevity, since my aim [here] is only the manifest, evident commandments. With all that we have recounted of them of these statements, they claim that they transmit, that they took from prophecy, that they are the people of the language, and that they are the [true] reasoners and doers. I shall later recount their claim in this and take up all that they claim for it — with its corruption. I now mention in the following bab some of their statements concerning the other commandments, of what amounts to abandoning the religion utterly and requires unbelief (kufr) and irreligion (ilḥād) — for in this too is an alerting to their case, and a refutation of what they claim of having transmitted from prophecy. ---
